title: Psychoeducational assessment — raw clinician notes (split model)
note:
RAW ASSESSMENT NOTES — for report writer. Assessor: M.Ed. level, in person. Client: Nadia Okonkwo-Reyes, DOB 2014-03-19, MRN-88214, 17 Fernbrook Lane, Barrie, ON. Mother reachable at 905-555-0164.

REFERRAL. Referred by her Grade 6 teacher at Bayfield Heights P.S. through the school team. Presenting concern is a persistent gap between how she presents verbally and what she produces on paper. Mother, Amara, reports homework taking two to three hours nightly for work the teacher says should take forty minutes. Father declined to attend; parents separated 2023. Previous vision and hearing screens normal, done at the Barrie clinic last spring.

BACKGROUND. Full-term, no birth complications. Early motor milestones on time, speech slightly late — first sentences around 2y6m per mother's recollection, no formal SLP involvement. No head injury, no seizures. No psychiatric history. Sleeps poorly, mother estimates six hours on school nights. Lives with mother and younger brother Tobi. Maternal uncle described as having had 'reading trouble all through school' and never finishing high school; no formal diagnosis in the family.

SCHOOL HISTORY. Grades 1 through 3 at a small independent school, moved to Bayfield Heights in Grade 4. Report cards from Grade 4 onward show consistent teacher comments about effort and participation being strong and written output being weak. No IEP currently. Was on an informal monitoring list in Grade 5 under Ms Halvorsen.

BEHAVIOURAL OBSERVATIONS. Two sessions, both mornings, 90 and 75 minutes. Arrived on time both days with mother. Rapport established quickly, chatty, made several jokes. Sustained attention good for verbal tasks — did not need redirection. On written and timed tasks she fidgeted, asked twice how much longer, and on the second day said 'I'm bad at this part' before starting. Pencil grip unusual, high and tight. Frequent erasing. Read task instructions aloud under her breath. Effort appeared genuine throughout; results considered a valid estimate of current functioning.

TEST DATA.
WISC-V. Full Scale IQ 104. Verbal Comprehension 121. Visual Spatial 108. Fluid Reasoning 112. Working Memory 86. Processing Speed 79. Subtests: Similarities 14, Vocabulary 15, Block Design 11, Visual Puzzles 12, Matrix Reasoning 12, Figure Weights 13, Digit Span 8, Picture Span 7, Coding 6, Symbol Search 7.
WIAT-4. Word Reading 92. Pseudoword Decoding 85. Reading Comprehension 108. Oral Reading Fluency 81. Spelling 84. Sentence Composition 88. Essay Composition 79. Math Problem Solving 110. Numerical Operations 101.
CTOPP-2. Phonological Awareness 88. Rapid Symbolic Naming 78. Phonological Memory 90.
BRIEF-2 parent form. Working Memory T=68. Plan/Organize T=64. Task Monitor T=66. Inhibit T=52. Emotional Control T=49.
Conners-3 teacher form. Inattention T=71. Hyperactivity/Impulsivity T=48. Learning Problems T=74.

ASSESSOR IMPRESSIONS, unstructured. The verbal-versus-output split is the whole picture here. She reasons well above average and expresses it fluently out loud, and then everything narrows the moment it has to go through decoding, spelling or speed. Processing Speed and Rapid Naming are the two lowest scores in the file and they are consistent with each other. Decoding weaker than comprehension, which is the classic pattern — she is comprehending by inference and vocabulary rather than by reading the words accurately. Essay Composition being the lowest academic score fits: that is the task that loads decoding, spelling, working memory and speed all at once.

Would want the report writer to consider SLD in reading (word-level) and written expression. The attention picture is muddier — teacher inattention elevated but hyperactivity normal, and the parent BRIEF elevations are all in the working memory and planning cluster rather than inhibition. Could be secondary to the learning profile rather than a separate ADHD presentation. Flagging for the psychologist's judgement, not asserting it.

Accommodations that came up in conversation with mother and worth considering: extra time, text-to-speech, speech-to-text for longer written work, spelling not penalised in content marks, and a reduced-volume homework agreement given the two-to-three hour figure.

Note for writer: mother asked directly whether this means Nadia 'isn't smart.' Worth addressing that explicitly and early in the parent-facing section. She also asked whether the uncle's history is relevant.
